contributions.headingText: Infantile haemangioma is a benign tumour characterized by a proliferation of lobules of capillaries with a distinctive immunophenotype arising exclusively in infancy and showing spontaneous slow regression.
2E81.2Y & XH3U29 Other specified benign vascular lesion of infancy and childhood & Capillary haemangioma
Not recommended: capillary haemangioma; juvenile haemangioma; strawberry naevus; capillary-cavernous haemangioma; infantile haemangioendothelioma.
These lesions are most common on the head and neck and the extremities, but they also occur on the trunk, genitals, and in some viscera (notably, the liver and intestines).

Nascent tumours may be evident at birth but typically appear in the first 2–6 weeks of life, as a bright-red or blue nodule or plaque, often with a strawberry-like appearance. There is initial rapid growth over a period of months, transitioning to a longer involuting phase of a few years {18429772; 24641194}. Lesions arising at certain locations may be associated with underlying malformations and multiple lesions; usually, the presence of > 5 lesions is associated with liver haemangiomas {34419524}.
This haemangioma, which occurs in about 4% of the population, is the most common tumour of infancy. It shows a female predilection and is more common in White populations {18429772; 24641194}.
Although racial distributions suggest genetic predilections, there is no evidence to support a primary genetic driver. Rare families show an increased incidence.

The fact that infantile haemangioma’s immunoreactivity for GLUT1, LeY, and other markers is identical to that of placental microvessels suggests that this tumour results from embolization of placental cells or stem cells differentiating towards placental vascular cells {11346333}. Cultured infantile haemangioma endothelial cells are clonal, a finding consistent with a neoplastic process {11254674}. No underlying genetic abnormalities have been identified.

The histology of infantile haemangioma defines the three stages of the lesion: proliferation, partial involution, and complete involution. These stages form an overlapping continuum. Early proliferative lesions consist of cellular dermal and/or subcutaneous masses of tightly packed capillaries with small lumina, lined by plump endothelial cells rimmed by pericytes. The capillaries are interspersed with immature dendritic-type cells and arranged in lobules separated by delicate fibrous septa or normal intervening stroma. Perineural extension is common {7737662}, and the feeding and draining vessels may be quite large. During active involution, the lesional capillaries become variably dilated and congested, and gradually disappear. The basement membranes thicken and show apoptotic dust, and the pericapillary mast cells increase in number. Nearing end-stage, the tumour lobules are replaced by loose fibrous or fibrofatty stroma containing a few residual ghost capillaries composed of thickened multilayered rinds of basement membrane material with little or no cellular lining. The endothelial cells show a complex immunophenotype shared only by placental capillaries, including positivity for GLUT1, LeY, CD15, CCR6, IDO1, and IGF2 {11735711}.

Differential diagnosis

Infantile haemangioma must be distinguished from congenital non-progressive haemangiomas on the basis of careful clinicopathological correlation and GLUT1 immunohistochemistry. All infantile haemangiomas have endothelial GLUT1 positivity, whereas congenital non-progressive haemangioma endothelial cells are negative for this marker {10665907}.
Essential: an acquired vascular tumour developing after birth and composed of lobules of capillaries lined by GLUT1-positive endothelial cells.
These tumours are benign, but treatment is necessary when there is associated morbidity due to location or size. All cases show spontaneous regression, albeit with variation in rate and degree.
